title: Order of Draw: Why EDTA Comes Late
summary: Fill six coloured tubes in the right order, watch a trace of EDTA ride the needle into a chemistry tube and send potassium up and calcium down, and learn to spot the fingerprint.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 3 Hit 1 (core: order of draw), Hit 5, Traps 1–2 and the Figure 3 order-of-draw illustration. Adds the WHO 2010 table (including the optional plain discard tube), the reversed skin-puncture order, experimental EDTA effects and the mixed evidence on carry-over with closed systems.

objectives: List the venipuncture order of draw: blood culture, citrate, serum, heparin, EDTA, fluoride.
Explain how additive carry-over makes the order matter, and why EDTA comes late.
Recognize the EDTA-contamination pattern (very high potassium, very low calcium and magnesium) and respond correctly.
State that skin punctures reverse the order (EDTA first).

scenes.title: A potassium that should not be possible
scenes.altText: A lab report card shows potassium 25 mmol/L flagged critically high and calcium near zero flagged critically low. Beside it, the patient token reads “sitting up, chatting”. The cartoon scientist frowns at the mismatch.

cues.text: A chemistry result comes back: potassium 25. A normal value is about 3.5 to 5.
Calcium is almost zero. Either number alone could stop a heart.
Yet the patient is sitting up and chatting. How can the blood say “dying” while the patient says “fine”?

scenes.title: The order of draw
scenes.altText: Six tubes with coloured stoppers appear one by one, left to right, each numbered: 1 blood culture (yellow), 2 citrate (light blue), 3 serum/SST (red or gold), 4 heparin (green), 5 EDTA (lavender), 6 fluoride/oxalate (grey). A needle token slides along above them, and a small arrow between each pair shows that a trace of additive can ride the needle into the next tube.

cues.text: One needle can fill many tubes. But a tiny trace of additive can cling to the needle and ride into the next tube. So the order matters.
First, blood cultures: they must stay sterile, so nothing goes in before them. Second, the light blue citrate tube for clotting tests, which other additives easily upset.
Third, serum tubes — plain red or gold gel tubes with clot activator. Fourth, green heparin tubes.
Fifth, lavender EDTA. EDTA grabs calcium, and it is a potassium salt, so it must come late, after the chemistry tubes.
Last, grey fluoride tubes, which keep cells from using up glucose.
Stopper colours can differ between makers, so labs follow their local chart. WHO also allows a plain discard tube before citrate when needed.

props.text: Additive can ride the needle into the next tube
Colours vary by maker — follow the local chart

scenes.title: EDTA in the wrong tube
scenes.altText: The lavender EDTA tube jumps ahead of the red serum tube. A drop of EDTA rides into the serum tube. Bars for potassium, calcium and magnesium respond: potassium rises; calcium and magnesium fall. A data card shows an experiment: with 5% EDTA blood mixed in, potassium +15%, calcium −12%, magnesium −23%; at 43%, potassium +175% and calcium −100%. A final card notes that careful closed-system studies did not always find carry-over, but contamination is still found in practice.

cues.text: Now break the rule. The lavender EDTA tube is drawn before the chemistry tube, and a trace of EDTA rides along.
EDTA comes as a potassium salt, so potassium goes up. And EDTA grabs calcium and magnesium, so they go down.
In one experiment, mixing in just 5 percent EDTA blood raised potassium 15 percent and cut calcium 12 percent. At 43 percent, potassium rose 175 percent and calcium disappeared.
So very high potassium with very low calcium, in a patient who looks well, is EDTA’s fingerprint. The reviewer’s classic example is potassium around 25.
Some careful studies with closed vacuum tubes found no carry-over from the wrong order alone. But contamination still turns up in practice, so the order of draw stays.

props.title: Experiment: EDTA blood mixed into heparin blood (Lima-Oliveira 2014)

props.label: Fingerprint: K⁺ very high + Ca²⁺ very low + patient well

props.text: Closed-system studies: carry-over not always found (Ercan 2021) — contamination still happens

scenes.title: In the lab: catch it, confirm it, recollect
scenes.altText: A decision path: “K⁺ 25 arrives” → “Check calcium (and magnesium)” → “Very low? Patient well?” → “Suspect EDTA contamination” → “Measure serum EDTA if available / request a new sample in the correct order”. Then a light blue tube with an EDTA drop and a clock showing a falsely long clotting time. Finally, a heel-stick panel shows the skin-puncture order reversed: EDTA first.

cues.text: In the lab, a potassium of 25 arrives. Before treating it as real, look at the calcium.
Potassium very high, calcium and magnesium very low, and a patient who is not ill? Suspect EDTA contamination.
Labs can confirm by measuring EDTA in the serum, where that test is available, and they ask for a new sample drawn in the right order — following the lab’s own critical-result policy.
The same rule protects clotting tests. The reviewer warns that EDTA carried into the light blue tube falsely prolongs PT and APTT — so blue always comes before lavender.
One twist: skin punctures use the reverse order. WHO says collect the hematology EDTA sample first, to limit platelet clumping, then chemistry and blood bank.

scenes.title: Two traps and one order
scenes.altText: Trap card: “Draw lavender before light blue” is crossed out → “Blue before lavender, always.” Trap card: “K⁺ 25 = call critical hyperkalemia” is crossed out → “Check Ca²⁺; suspect EDTA; recollect per policy.” Then the six stoppers line up again in order.

cues.text: Trap one: “Drawing lavender before light blue is fine.” No — EDTA carried into the citrate tube upsets the clotting tests. Blue before lavender, always.
Trap two: “Potassium 25 means call critical hyperkalemia right away.” First check calcium — if it is near zero in a well patient, suspect EDTA and ask for a new sample, following your lab’s policy.
And the order itself: culture, citrate, serum, heparin, EDTA, fluoride.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: The six stoppers in order, with a small EDTA drop crossed out between lavender and the earlier tubes.

cues.text: Draw blood culture, citrate, serum, heparin, EDTA and then fluoride, because additives can ride the needle into the next tube — and a sky-high potassium with near-zero calcium in a well patient points to EDTA contamination, not a dying patient.

props.text: K⁺ ↑↑ + Ca²⁺ ↓↓ + well patient → think EDTA

explanation.what: Plain language: when one needle fills several tubes, a tiny bit of the chemical in one tube can sneak into the next, so tubes are filled in a set order. Scientific terms: the venipuncture order of draw is blood culture → sodium citrate (light blue) → serum tubes (plain red or gel/SST with clot activator) → heparin (green) → EDTA (lavender) → sodium fluoride/potassium oxalate (grey). It minimizes additive carry-over between tubes.
explanation.why: Blood cultures go first to stay sterile. Citrate is early because coagulation tests are easily disturbed by other additives. K2/K3 EDTA is a potassium salt that chelates calcium and magnesium, so EDTA carried into a serum or heparin tube raises potassium and lowers calcium and magnesium; it is therefore drawn after the chemistry tubes. Fluoride goes last.
explanation.measure: The lab sees the effect as spurious hyperkalemia with hypocalcemia (and hypomagnesemia). In an experiment, 5% EDTA blood raised potassium 15% and cut calcium 12%; 43% EDTA raised potassium 175% and abolished calcium. Labs confirm suspected contamination with a serum EDTA assay where available and recollect.
explanation.differs: True hyperkalemia vs EDTA contamination: contamination brings very low calcium and magnesium and does not fit the patient. Venipuncture order vs skin-puncture order: skin punctures collect EDTA (hematology) first to limit platelet clumping. Citrate vs EDTA: both remove calcium, but they serve different tests.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: put the tubes in order, “which tube is drawn immediately before EDTA?” (heparin), “why is EDTA drawn after the SST?” (potassium and calcium interference), a K⁺ ≈ 25 with Ca²⁺ ≈ 0 case (EDTA contamination, recollect), and the reversed skin-puncture order.

comparisons.title: True hyperkalemia vs EDTA contamination

left.label: True hyperkalemia
points: Fits the clinical picture (e.g., kidney failure)

right.label: EDTA contamination
points: Patient looks well; values often impossible

comparisons.distinguisher: Look at calcium: EDTA drags it down while pushing potassium up.

comparisons.title: Venipuncture vs skin-puncture order

left.label: Venipuncture
points: Culture → citrate → serum → heparin → EDTA → fluoride

right.label: Skin puncture
points: Then chemistry and blood bank; limits platelet clumping

comparisons.distinguisher: Skin punctures reverse the order because clotting starts at the puncture site.

mnemonic.explanation: Culture, Citrate, Serum, Heparin, EDTA, Grey fluoride — the venipuncture order of draw.
mnemonic.limitation: It does not apply to skin punctures, which reverse the order. Stopper colours vary between manufacturers, and full charts include extra tubes (a plain discard tube, gel heparin, ACD) that the six words leave out.

analogyLimitations: The needle “carrying” a visible drop exaggerates carry-over, which is microscopic.
Stopper colours shown are common ones; local colour codes can differ.
The K⁺ 25 / Ca²⁺ 0.3 report is an illustrative case built on the reviewer’s example.
takeaway: Draw blood culture, citrate, serum, heparin, EDTA and then fluoride, because additives can ride the needle into the next tube — and a sky-high potassium with near-zero calcium in a well patient points to EDTA contamination, not a dying patient.

questions.stem: Which sequence shows the correct venipuncture order of draw?

options.text: Blood culture → citrate → serum (SST) → heparin → EDTA → fluoride
options.rationale: Correct. Sterile cultures first, citrate before other additives, EDTA after the chemistry tubes, fluoride last.

options.text: Citrate → blood culture → EDTA → serum → heparin → fluoride
options.rationale: Incorrect. Cultures come first to stay sterile, and EDTA before serum risks potassium and calcium errors.

options.text: EDTA → citrate → serum → heparin → fluoride → blood culture
options.rationale: Incorrect. This resembles the skin-puncture idea (EDTA first) but venipuncture puts EDTA late and cultures first.

options.text: Blood culture → EDTA → citrate → heparin → serum → fluoride
options.rationale: Incorrect. EDTA before citrate and serum tubes can contaminate coagulation and chemistry samples.

questions.stem: A well-appearing outpatient has potassium 11.8 mmol/L, calcium 0.4 mmol/L and low magnesium. The phlebotomist drew the lavender tube before the gold SST. What is the best response?

options.text: Suspect EDTA contamination, follow the lab’s critical-result policy, and request a new sample drawn in the correct order
options.rationale: Correct. Very high potassium with very low calcium and magnesium in a well patient, after EDTA was drawn first, is the contamination pattern.

options.text: Report it as true critical hyperkalemia with no comment
options.rationale: Incorrect. The pattern and the draw history point to contamination; reporting without comment could lead to harmful treatment.

options.text: Dilute the sample and repeat to get the true potassium
options.rationale: Incorrect. Dilution does not remove EDTA; the sample itself is compromised.

options.text: Add calcium to the sample to correct the result
options.rationale: Incorrect. Laboratories do not “correct” a contaminated specimen; it must be recollected.

questions.stem: For a capillary (skin) puncture needing a CBC and chemistry tests, which sample is collected first?

options.rationale: Correct. WHO advises collecting the hematology specimen first in skin punctures, to limit platelet clumping — the reverse of venipuncture.

options.text: The chemistry sample, as in venipuncture
options.rationale: Incorrect. Skin punctures reverse the venipuncture order.
Incorrect. WHO lists blood bank after hematology and chemistry for skin punctures.

options.text: Order does not matter for skin punctures
options.rationale: Incorrect. Platelets clump as the puncture clots, so the hematology sample goes first.

references.usedFor: 5% K2EDTA contamination: potassium +15%, calcium −12%, magnesium −23%; 43%: potassium +175%, calcium −100%; cites EDTA contamination as the cause of 14.3% of hypocalcaemia cases; serum EDTA assays can detect it.

references.usedFor: With a closed vacuum system, incorrect order of draw did not cause detectable K-EDTA contamination in routine workflow, although potassium differed between tubes.

claims.text: Venipuncture order: blood culture → citrate → serum (clot activator/SST) → heparin → EDTA → fluoride/oxalate, to avoid additive carry-over; colour codes vary locally.
Skin punctures reverse the order: the hematology (EDTA) specimen first, then chemistry and blood bank, to limit platelet clumping.
K2EDTA contamination raises potassium and lowers calcium and magnesium in a dose-dependent way (5%: K +15%, Ca −12%, Mg −23%; 43%: K +175%, Ca −100%).
Serum EDTA assays can confirm contamination; EDTA contamination has been reported as the cause of a notable share of low-calcium results.
With closed vacuum systems, wrong order alone did not always produce detectable EDTA carry-over.
EDTA contamination can produce potassium around 25 mEq/L with calcium near zero.
claims.note: The pattern is checked; the specific value is the reviewer’s example.

claims.text: EDTA carried into the citrate tube falsely prolongs PT/APTT.
claims.note: WHO supports avoiding additive cross-contamination generally; this specific effect was not stated in the sources read.

claims.text: Visible “drop” of carried-over additive and the illustrative K⁺ 25 report.

accuracyFlags.issue: The reviewer presents carry-over as certain; some closed-system studies found no detectable EDTA carry-over from wrong order alone (register flag rv-order-draw-evidence).
accuracyFlags.resolution: Lesson states the mixed evidence and why the order is still recommended.

accuracyFlags.issue: The K⁺ ≈ 25 mEq/L figure and the PT/APTT effect are not confirmed by the sources read.
